node-1.label: 14-year-old female presented with a two-month history of itchy skin lesions located on the upper and lower extremities, thighs, and pubic area

node-2.label: Physical examination showed well-demarcated annular brownish plaques measuring 5-7 cm, with scaly elevated borders, a few pustules on the upper and lower extremities, thighs, and pubic area, and central clearing in some lesions

node-3.label: System review revealed no other complaints, and there were no abnormalities in the hair, nails, mucosal, or genital areas

node-4.label: The patient was treated with terbinafine 250 mg tablets and topical miconazole cream applied twice daily for two weeks; at two-week follow-up, additional lesions were observed on the lower extremity and inner thigh despite adherence to the prescribed treatment

attrs.why: New biopsy evidence shows PAS-negative subcorneal pustules with neutrophils, eosinophils, acantholysis, and spongiosis. The laboratory physician and pathologist both state this refutes dermatophyte infection and that resistant tinea is unlikely without fungal elements. Although annular scaly plaques and central clearing initially supported dermatophyte infection, the negative PAS and antifungal treatment failure make dermatophyte skin infection very unlikely, reducing confidence from 0.5 to 0.05.

New PAS-negative biopsy shows no fungal elements; expert analyses from the laboratory physician and pathologist indicate resistant dermatophyte is unlikely. Progression despite terbinafine/miconazole is no longer sufficient to support a resistant fungal infection in the absence of mycological or histopathological evidence, reducing confidence from 0.3 to 0.05.

New biopsy evidence of PAS-negative subcorneal pustules with neutrophils, a few eosinophils, acantholysis, and spongiosis, plus failure of oral terbinafine and topical miconazole, is favored by both the laboratory physician and pathologist as an inflammatory pustular dermatosis. This directly supports an inflammatory rather than fungal process, raising confidence from 0.2 to 0.85.

node-8.label: Skin biopsy shows subcorneal pustules containing neutrophils with a few eosinophils, acantholytic cells, and spongiosis

node-9.label: PAS stain on skin biopsy is negative for fungal elements

attrs.why: Pathologist analysis confirms that PAS-negative subcorneal pustules with neutrophils/eosinophils, acantholysis, spongiosis, and failure of terbinafine/miconazole favor inflammatory pustular dermatosis and specifically Sneddon-Wilkinson disease. No new positive fungal or autoimmune test has emerged, so the working diagnosis remains at 0.85.

node-11.label: DIF and serum desmoglein/IgA anti-desmocollin tests remain unretrieved at step limit

attrs.why: Pathologist analysis emphasizes that DIF, desmoglein/IgA anti-desmocollin, and SPEP/immunofixation remain unretrieved, and that IgA pemphigus/paraproteinemic subcorneal pustulosis cannot be excluded. This keeps an autoimmune/paraproteinemic blistering process as a moderate alternative, but the pathologist favors inflammatory pustular dermatosis, so confidence remains 0.4.

Pathologist analysis explicitly states that PAS-negative subcorneal pustules with neutrophils/eosinophils, acantholysis, and spongiosis plus failure of terbinafine/miconazole favor an inflammatory pustular dermatosis and are likely Sneddon-Wilkinson disease. The SPEP/immunofixation, DIF, and desmoglein/IgA anti-desmocollin tests remain unretrieved, so other subcorneal pustular entities such as IgA pemphigus/paraproteinemic subcorneal pustulosis cannot be excluded. The specific histologic support raises confidence from 0.4 to 0.6.

Pathologist analysis notes that IgA pemphigus cannot be excluded and that IgA anti-desmocollin/DIF tests remain unretrieved. However, no positive IgA serology or DIF is available, and the pathologist favors Sneddon-Wilkinson disease; thus confidence remains 0.35.

Pathologist analysis favors Sneddon-Wilkinson disease based on subcorneal pustules with acantholysis and spongiosis, which is atypical for psoriasis. No psoriasiform epidermal changes are reported. Annular pustular psoriasis remains possible but less likely, so confidence is reduced from 0.25 to 0.2.

Refines 'Inflammatory dermatosis' (node-7) and the pemphigus-spectrum branch (node-12). Acantholysis with subcorneal pustulation and eosinophils (node-8) plus the pending DIF/desmoglein testing (node-11) keep an acantholytic autoimmune process plausible, but the prominent annular pustular plaques (node-2) and neutrophil-rich pustules are less typical, so confidence is lower.
